newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian prosecutors release some MinFin bonds.
newsitem.headline: Russian prosecutors release some MinFin bonds.

text.p: Russian prosecutors acted on Wednesday to end a scandal involving domestic bonds as preparations for Russia's first international bond since the 1917 revolution moved into a final phase.

Prosecutor-General Yuri Skuratov issued an order to review all cases where MinFin bonds had been frozen by the authorities, and to release them if they had been acquired in good faith, the official Itar-Tass agency said.

The dollar-denominated bonds, which run in several maturities from a few years to 2008, and pay three percent annual interest, were first issued in 1993 to companies whose foreign exchange accounts at the former Soviet foreign trade bank Vneshekonombank had been frozen.
Some district prosecutors have already started to release bonds. In Moscow's Tagansk district alone, the prosecutor had unfrozen $21 million of paper, Tass said.
The announcement pushed up MinFin bond prices in Moscow.

The seizures of the bonds, mostly related to investigations into thefts and embezzlements, outraged foreign bankers who said the freezing called into question Russia's whole attitude to investor rights.
Earlier this month a detective in Moscow's fifth central Moscow police precinct said his local prosecutor's office had ordered $57 million of bonds to be frozen in June.
The finance ministry had issued a list in July of $24 million of bonds which had been frozen, some of which had been stolen in the breakaway region of Chechnya.
Because $7 million of bonds are on both lists, the total now known to have been seized comes to $74 million.
Around $11 billion of the bonds are now in circulation and a lively market has arisen, both in Moscow and in foreign financial centres such as London, Paris and New York.
Prices were hit in the early summer when rumours first began to circulate that bonds had been frozen.
But they have since recovered on optimism about Russia's forthcoming Eurobond issue, likely before the end of the month.

A series of presentations by top Russian officials to potential international investors in the bond, the first time Russia is tapping international capital markets since the Tsarist era, ends on Wednesday in New York.

Attendance at the roadshow has been enthusiastic, and syndicate managers in London said Russia's debut offering could be as high as $750 million, rather than the previously mooted $500 million maximum.
Foreign investors are keen to buy a chunk of the Russian economy if they can avoid the settlement and custody risks which the MinFin bonds illustrate.

An American Depositary Receipt (ADR) issue by Moscow mobile phone operator Vimpel Communications last week jumped nearly 40 percent to $28-7/8 at its debut on Wall Street last Thursday, making it the top performer on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Eurobond will be governed by international law and placed in international custody, so it would not be subject to the same risks as the MinFin bonds.

But Russian officials are keen to clear up the mess. Earlier this month the government called on the judicial authorities to review the freezings, and draw up proposals to eliminate contradictions in Russian law which they exposed.

Russian's Civil Code says bearer securities, including MinFin bonds, cannot be seized if they were acquired in good faith, but the Criminal Code says they can be seized in the course of an investigation into a suspected crime.
